articles.title: We re-priced six weeks of our own AI coding-agent usage. The "obvious" saving was 5.5x too big.
articles.excerpt: Over 46 days (35 of them active), one person's coding agent made 61,955 requests. There was no invoice for this exercise - a real client audit starts by reconciling to one - so we did what you do with…
articles.body: Over 46 days (35 of them active), one person's coding agent made 61,955 requests . There was no invoice for this exercise - a real client audit starts by reconciling to one - so we did what you do without one: we re-priced every request at the vendor's public, dated price sheet (retrieved 2026-10-16) and asked where the money would go. Every dollar figure below is API-equivalent , not what anyone was billed. The total came to $7,882 . Three things in it surprised us. 1. Almost all of it is re-reading 66% of the cost was cache reads , and 99% of input-side tokens were cache hits. Output - the thing people optimise prompts for - was 12%. Spend is driven by how long the context is x how many turns run on it , and one project accounted for 63% of it.

articles.excerpt: I've recently been spending some time exploring HL7, FHIR and the broader healthcare interoperability landscape—particularly how standards, implementation approaches and validation come together in pr…
articles.body: I've recently been spending some time exploring HL7, FHIR and the broader healthcare interoperability landscape —particularly how standards, implementation approaches and validation come together in practice. As I organized some of those thoughts, another connection became increasingly interesting: What happens when healthcare interoperability meets AI? At first, these can seem like two separate conversations. FHIR and HL7 help establish structure, meaning and consistency in how healthcare information is exchanged. AI brings capabilities around language, reasoning, knowledge discovery and, increasingly, action. The more I explored the two, the more interesting their intersection became.
articles.author: Abhi Chatterjee

articles.title: I let a one-shot Sonnet 5 agent QA a live app. Then I ran our QA tool on the same one.
articles.excerpt: Every week, someone tells me our company shouldn't exist. So we stopped arguing and ran the experiment. We took a real, production EU rail-booking app. We turned a strong Sonnet 5 agent loose on it —…
articles.body: Every week, someone tells me our company shouldn't exist. The line is always some version of this: "QA? I'll just point Claude or Sonnet at my app." And honestly — it's a fair shot. These models are good. If a one-shot agent already does what we do, then we're selling snake oil. So we stopped arguing and ran the experiment. We took a real, production EU rail-booking app. We turned a strong Sonnet 5 agent loose on it — from scratch, no hand-holding — to hunt bugs and write tests the way a sharp QA engineer would. Then we ran our own tool, TestOptim , through its full pipeline on the exact same app. Then we handed both outputs, unlabelled, to an independent judge and asked one question: which is better, and why?

articles.title: I went quiet. The mascot would call this a comeback.

articles.body: My last post ended on this line: "The rail decides whether that holds." It did not hold. That was 29 August. Today is 16 October. Seven weeks without a post, on a blog where I once promised one every Friday. When I missed a single Friday back in June, I wrote that the story I tell myself about a miss does more damage than the miss itself. So I am not going to count the weeks again, and I am not announcing a fresh start. I built something that has an opinion about exactly this situation, and I am going to take its advice. the mascot does not count either Momentum Mascot has four moods: awake, dozing, asleep, and comeback. When a project goes quiet, the character goes to bed. It does not die, nothing breaks, and nothing tells you how long it has been.

articles.title: 5 Slurm Configuration Parameters That Shape Your HPC Cluster
articles.excerpt: When building an HPC cluster, we often focus on compute nodes, CPUs, RAM, GPUs, networking and storage. But there is another important part of the design: how Slurm manages those resources. A cluster…
articles.body: When building an HPC cluster, we often focus on compute nodes, CPUs, RAM, GPUs, networking and storage. But there is another important part of the design: how Slurm manages those resources. A cluster might have hundreds of CPU cores and several GPUs, but how effectively users access those resources depends partly on how Slurm is configured. Let's explore five important configuration areas in slurm.conf and understand their impact on an HPC environment. 1. SelectType and SelectTypeParameters These parameters control how Slurm selects resources and allocates them to jobs. For example: SelectType = select/cons_tres SelectTypeParameters = CR_Core select/cons_tres allows Slurm to track and allocate consumable resources, such as CPUs, memory and GPUs when configured appropriately.

articles.title: Why can you see the moon during the day? This week is the perfect time to find out
articles.excerpt: You don't have to wait until dark to see the moon. Here's why it appears in broad daylight — and why this week is a particularly good time to spot it.
articles.body: I know perfectly well that the moon comes out during the day. I have known this for decades. Yet whenever I spot it in a blue afternoon sky, some primitive part of my brain still thinks it has turned up early. I'm certainly not the only one. Many people don't understand how it could be visible in daylight. In their eyes, the moon is a nighttime object. Why? Because that's when they notice it — it appears brighter. We tend to think of the sun as belonging to the day and the moon to the night because that's how they're usually presented to us as children. Astronomically, it makes little sense. The moon spends plenty of time above our horizon while the sun is also up — it spends half its time in the daytime sky, in fact.
